questions.prompt: Explain three differences between a typical photosynthetic plant cell and a bacterial cell.
scheme: 1 · Plant DNA is enclosed in a nucleus; bacterial DNA is not.
2 · The plant cell has chloroplasts; the bacterium does not.
3 · The plant cell has a permanent vacuole; the bacterium does not.

questions.prompt: A cell is 50 μm across. A bacterium is 0.5 μm across. Calculate how many orders of magnitude larger the cell is.
scheme: 2 · 100 = 10², so two orders of magnitude.

questions.prompt: Describe the functions of four structures found in a palisade leaf cell.
scheme: 1 · Nucleus contains genetic material that controls the cell.
2 · Chloroplasts absorb light for photosynthesis.
3 · Cellulose cell wall strengthens/supports the cell.
4 · Permanent vacuole contains cell sap / keeps the cell turgid. Accept mitochondria for respiration, ribosomes for protein synthesis, membrane controls movement of substances.

questions.prompt: Which structure makes proteins?
options: Mitochondrion
Ribosome
Cell wall
Cell membrane
scheme: Ribosomes join amino acids together to make proteins. Mitochondria release energy, the cell wall supports the cell and the membrane controls what enters and leaves.

questions.prompt: Where is the main bacterial DNA?
options: Free in the cytoplasm as a single loop
Inside a nucleus surrounded by a membrane
Inside a chloroplast in the middle of the cell
Packed inside a vacuole in the cytoplasm
scheme: Bacteria are prokaryotes, so their main DNA is a single loop lying free in the cytoplasm rather than inside a nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
options: A cell membrane that controls what enters the cell
A ribosome where proteins are made in the cytoplasm
A cell wall made of cellulose that strengthens the cell
A mitochondrion where respiration releases energy
scheme: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall; animal cells do not. The other structures are found in both.

questions.prompt: What is a plasmid?
options: A protein-making organelle found in the cytoplasm of cells
The fluid-filled space inside a large plant cell vacuole
A type of cell wall made of cellulose in plant cells
A small ring of DNA found in many bacterial cells
scheme: Plasmids are small extra rings of DNA in many bacteria, separate from the main loop of DNA.

questions.prompt: Bacteria are described as prokaryotic because…
options: they have no cell membrane around the cytoplasm
they contain chloroplasts, which plant cells also have
their genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus
they always cause disease when they enter the body
scheme: Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus; their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm.

questions.prompt: Which organelle releases most of the energy from aerobic respiration?
options: Nucleus
Mitochondrion
Permanent vacuole
Ribosome
scheme: Aerobic respiration takes place mainly in mitochondria.

questions.prompt: A bacterial cell is 2 µm long. A human cheek cell is 60 µm across. Give 2 µm in metres in standard form.
A bacterial cell is 2 µm long. A human cheek cell is 60 µm across. Calculate how many times longer the cheek cell is than the bacterium.
A bacterial cell is 2 µm long. A human cheek cell is 60 µm across. Name the structure in the cheek cell that controls the activities of the cell, and explain why bacteria do not have this structure.
scheme: 1 · nucleus; bacteria are prokaryotes (DNA free in cytoplasm)

questions.prompt: A cell image is 54 mm wide at ×1800. Calculate actual width in micrometres.
scheme: 1 · Actual size = image size / magnification.

questions.prompt: A student draws a cheek cell 60 mm wide. The real cell is 60 μm wide. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
Compare light microscopes and electron microscopes. Explain how electron microscopy has improved our understanding of cells.
scheme: 1 · Electron microscopes have higher magnification.
2 · Electron microscopes have higher resolution / can distinguish two points closer together.
3 · So smaller subcellular structures (e.g. ribosomes, internal structure of mitochondria/chloroplasts) can be seen.
4 · Light microscopes are cheaper/portable and can view living specimens in colour.

questions.prompt: A 20 μm cell appears 40 mm long. Calculate magnification.
What distinguishes two close organelles?
options: High resolution
Bright staining dyes
A larger printed image
A lower magnification
scheme: Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close objects as separate. Magnification only makes an image larger.

questions.prompt: An image is 12 mm long. The real object is 0.03 mm long. What is the magnification?
How many micrometres are in 1 mm?
Which of these can only be seen clearly with an electron microscope?
options: Nucleus
Cell wall
Ribosomes
Chloroplasts
scheme: Ribosomes are too small to resolve with a light microscope.

questions.prompt: Write 0.000 005 m in standard form.
scheme: Move the decimal point 6 places: 5 × 10⁻⁶ m.

questions.prompt: A student views onion epidermis cells with a light microscope. Give the reason for adding iodine solution to the onion cells.
scheme: 1 · to stain the cells / make the nucleus (structures) visible

questions.prompt: A student views onion epidermis cells with a light microscope. The eyepiece lens is ×10 and the objective lens is ×10. A cell measures 25 mm in the student’s drawing. Calculate the real length of the cell in µm.
scheme: 1 · magnification = 100

questions.prompt: Explain three adaptations of a sperm cell for fertilisation.
scheme: 1 · A tail allows movement towards an egg.
2 · Many mitochondria support respiration for movement.
3 · Enzymes in the head help penetrate egg coverings.

questions.prompt: Explain why most animal cells lose the ability to differentiate, while many plant cells keep it.
scheme: 1 · Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage; in adults division is mainly for repair/replacement.
2 · Plants have meristems / continue growing throughout life, so they keep producing new specialised cells.

questions.prompt: Describe how a nerve cell and a root hair cell are each adapted to their function.
scheme: 1 · Nerve cell has a long axon to carry impulses over long distances.
2 · Nerve cell has branched endings/dendrites to connect with many cells.
3 · Root hair cell has a long extension giving a large surface area.
4 · For absorbing water and mineral ions (faster) / many mitochondria for active transport.

questions.prompt: What is differentiation?
options: Developing specialised cell structures so a cell can do a particular job
All of the cells in an organism losing their DNA as they develop
Fusion of a sperm and an egg cell to form a zygote cell
Division of one cell into two genetically identical daughter cells
scheme: Differentiation is how a cell gains the structures it needs to do one job.

questions.prompt: Why is a root hair useful?
options: It makes the root surface photosynthesise in the soil
It increases the surface area for absorbing water and minerals
It prevents mineral ions from being taken up by the root
It stores starch for the plant to use in the winter
scheme: Root hair cells have a large surface area, so water and mineral ions are absorbed faster.

questions.prompt: Why does a sperm cell contain many mitochondria?
options: To release energy by respiration so that the tail can swim
To store food for the embryo after the sperm has fused
To make the cell wall that surrounds the sperm nucleus
To carry the genetic material that is passed to the egg
scheme: Respiration in mitochondria releases the energy a sperm needs to swim to the egg.

questions.prompt: Why do root hair cells usually lack chloroplasts?
options: They are too small to contain any organelles at all
They are dead cells, so they have no organelles inside them
Chloroplasts would block the movement of water into the cell
They are underground and receive no light
scheme: No light reaches roots, so chloroplasts would be of no use there.

questions.prompt: Which describes differentiation?
options: A cell divides into two cells that are genetically identical
A cell loses its nucleus so that it can carry more oxygen
A cell gains new structures so that it can do a particular job
A cell takes in water across its membrane by osmosis alone
scheme: Differentiation is the process of a cell becoming specialised for a job.

questions.prompt: What do the branched dendrites of a nerve cell do?
options: Store fat that the cell can use as a source of energy
Contract to move bones when an impulse arrives at the cell
Absorb mineral ions from the soil for the nerve cell to use
Connect with many other nerve cells so impulses are passed on
scheme: Branched dendrites let a neurone receive impulses from many other cells.

questions.prompt: Root hair cells absorb water and mineral ions from the soil. Explain how the shape of a root hair cell is adapted for absorption.
scheme: 1 · long thin projection / large surface area
1 · so more water and ions can be absorbed

questions.prompt: Root hair cells absorb water and mineral ions from the soil. Suggest why a plant may wilt if many of its root hairs are damaged when it is moved.
scheme: 1 · smaller surface area for absorbing water, so less water is taken up than is lost

questions.prompt: Describe how the cell cycle produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
scheme: 1 · DNA is replicated before division.
2 · Copies of each chromosome separate to opposite ends and nuclei divide.
3 · Cytoplasm and membrane divide, leaving identical chromosome sets.

questions.prompt: Give two ways a cell prepares for division before mitosis.
scheme: 1 · It grows / increases the number of subcellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria.
2 · It copies/replicates its DNA so each chromosome forms two copies.

questions.prompt: A scientist counts cells in an onion root tip: 380 cells not dividing and 20 cells in mitosis. The cell cycle takes 24 hours. Calculate the time spent in mitosis in minutes, and explain why the root tip is a good place to look.
scheme: 1 · Total cells = 400.
3 · = 72 minutes.
4 · Root tips contain meristem cells that divide frequently.

questions.prompt: Three cells each complete two rounds of division. How many result?
What happens before mitosis?
options: DNA is copied so there are two sets of genetic material
Chromosomes halve in number to make two gamete cells
Gametes fuse together to form a new fertilised egg cell
The cell wall breaks down so that the nucleus can escape
scheme: Before mitosis the cell grows and copies its DNA, so each daughter cell can receive a full set of chromosomes.

questions.prompt: How many chromosomes are in a human skin cell after mitosis?
scheme: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same.

questions.prompt: Why must DNA be copied before mitosis?
options: So the cell can grow a new cell wall around itself
To halve the chromosome number ready for fertilisation
To make the cell specialised for one particular job
So each daughter cell receives a full set of chromosomes
scheme: Each new cell needs complete genetic information, so the DNA must be copied first.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a use of mitosis?
options: Producing gametes
Growth
Repair of damaged tissue
Asexual reproduction
scheme: Gametes are produced by meiosis.

questions.prompt: One cell divides by mitosis five times. How many cells result?
scheme: Each division doubles the number of cells, so five divisions give 2⁵ = 32 cells.

questions.prompt: Bacteria and body cells both divide, but in different ways. A cell has 46 chromosomes. Give the number of chromosomes in each daughter cell after mitosis.
Bacteria and body cells both divide, but in different ways. A cell divides every 20 minutes. Calculate how many cells there are after 2 hours, starting from one cell.
scheme: 1 · 6 divisions
1 · 2⁶ = 64 cells

b-stem.title: Stem cells: benefits, risks and ethics

questions.prompt: Evaluate embryonic stem cells for replacing damaged nerve tissue.
scheme: 1 · They can differentiate into a wider range of cell types than many adult stem cells.
2 · A biological risk such as infection or uncontrolled division must be considered.
3 · Potential treatment benefit must be weighed against ethical concerns about embryo use.

questions.prompt: Describe how plant meristem tissue can be used to save a rare plant species from extinction.
scheme: 1 · Meristem cells are removed from root/shoot tip.
2 · Grown on a medium/in sterile conditions to form many clones.
3 · Clones are identical, quickly produced and can be replanted/stored.

questions.prompt: Stem cells from embryos could be used to treat type 1 diabetes. Evaluate this use of stem cells.
scheme: 1 · Stem cells could be differentiated into insulin-producing pancreas cells.
2 · This could cure the condition / remove the need for insulin injections.
3 · Therapeutic cloning gives cells that are not rejected by the immune system.
4 · Risk of transferring viral infection from cultured cells.
5 · Risk of cells dividing uncontrollably / tumours.
6 · Ethical/religious objections to using embryos, with a justified conclusion.

questions.prompt: Where are adult human stem cells found?
options: Mature red blood cells in the circulation
Tooth enamel on the surface of the teeth
Bone marrow, where blood cells are made
The outer layers of the skin that are shed
scheme: Adult stem cells are found in places such as bone marrow, where they make new blood cells.

questions.prompt: Why use genetically matched stem cells?
options: To reduce the chance that the body rejects the cells
To remove every protein from the transplanted tissue
To prevent all of the cells from dividing again
To make the transplanted cells grow more slowly
scheme: Genetically matched cells carry the patient's own markers, so the immune system does not attack them.

questions.prompt: Where are meristems found in a plant?
options: Only in the leaves where photosynthesis takes place
At the tips of the roots and the shoots of a plant
Only in the flowers where the seeds are produced
In the xylem vessels that carry water upwards
scheme: Meristems are regions of active cell division at root and shoot tips.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of therapeutic cloning?
options: The stem cells match the patient, so they are not rejected
It is cheap, because no equipment or laboratory is needed
It never involves embryos, so there are no ethical concerns
It produces gametes that can be used for fertility treatment
scheme: Cells made by therapeutic cloning carry the patient's own genes, so the body does not reject them.

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of stem-cell treatment?
options: Cells always die
Treatment cannot be repeated
Cells are too large to inject
Transfer of viral infection
scheme: Contaminated cultures could transfer viruses.

questions.prompt: Which cell type can adult bone marrow stem cells form?
options: Nerve cells only
Any cell type
Blood cells
Plant cells
scheme: Bone marrow stem cells produce a limited range, including blood cells.

questions.prompt: Explain why alveoli exchange gases rapidly.
scheme: 1 · Many alveoli provide a large surface area.
2 · Thin walls give a short diffusion distance.
3 · Ventilation and blood flow maintain concentration gradients.

questions.prompt: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube of side 5 mm. Give your answer as a ratio x : 1.
scheme: 1 · Surface area = 6 × 25 = 150 mm².
2 · Volume = 125 mm³.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of villi in the small intestine increases the rate of absorption of digested food.
scheme: 1 · Villi (and microvilli) give a large surface area.
2 · Wall is one cell thick / short diffusion distance.
3 · Rich capillary network carries absorbed molecules away.
4 · Which maintains a steep concentration gradient. Accept many mitochondria for active transport.

questions.prompt: A cube has side 2 cm. Express its surface area to volume ratio as x:1.
scheme: Area 24 cm²; volume 8 cm³; 24:8 = 3:1.

questions.prompt: Which change speeds diffusion?
options: A steeper concentration gradient
A thicker barrier between the two sides
A smaller surface area for the exchange
A lower temperature of the surroundings
scheme: A steeper concentration gradient gives a faster net movement of particles.

questions.prompt: What is the SA:V of a 3 cm cube?
scheme: Area 54 cm², volume 27 cm³; 54 ÷ 27 = 2.

questions.prompt: How do fish gills maintain a steep concentration gradient?
options: The gills are thick, which keeps the oxygen in
The water does not move over the gills at all
Blood flows in the opposite direction to the water
The gills have no blood supply, so oxygen builds up
scheme: Counter-current flow keeps a concentration gradient along the whole length of the gill.

questions.prompt: Which change would halve the rate of diffusion across a membrane?
options: Doubling the surface area
Doubling the concentration difference
Raising the temperature
Doubling the membrane thickness
scheme: Rate is inversely proportional to the diffusion distance.

questions.prompt: Why do single-celled organisms not need a gas exchange system?
options: They have a large surface area to volume ratio
They do not respire, so they do not need any oxygen
They are too small to need any oxygen to survive
They use active transport only, because it is faster
scheme: A large surface area to volume ratio means diffusion across the membrane meets their needs.

questions.prompt: Fish gills are an exchange surface. Give two features of gills that make gas exchange efficient.
scheme: 1 · large surface area (many filaments / lamellae)
1 · thin / short diffusion distance / good blood supply / water flow maintains gradient

questions.prompt: Explain why potato tissue loses mass in concentrated sugar solution.
scheme: 1 · The outside solution is more concentrated than the cell contents.
2 · Water moves out by osmosis across partially permeable cell membranes.
3 · Water loss reduces tissue mass.

questions.prompt: Explain why potato cylinders should be blotted dry before reweighing.
scheme: 1 · Removes surface solution/water.
2 · So the mass measured is only that of the tissue / measurements are comparable.

questions.prompt: Describe a method to find the concentration of sucrose solution with the same water concentration as potato cells.
scheme: 1 · Cut potato cylinders of the same size/with the same borer and length.
2 · Blot and weigh each cylinder.
3 · Place in a range of sucrose concentrations, e.g. 0 to 1.0 mol/dm³.
4 · Leave for the same time at the same temperature.
5 · Remove, blot dry in the same way and reweigh; calculate percentage change.
6 · Plot % change against concentration; where the line crosses zero is the answer.

questions.prompt: A cylinder changes from 4.0 g to 3.6 g. Calculate percentage mass change.
When does water enter a cell by osmosis?
options: The solution outside is more concentrated than the cell contents
The solution outside is more dilute than the cell contents
Water can never cross a partially permeable membrane
The cell contents have exactly the same concentration as outside
scheme: Water moves by osmosis from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one, so it enters when the outside is more dilute.

questions.prompt: A potato piece goes from 2.50 g to 2.00 g. What is the percentage change?
Why might a red blood cell burst in pure water?
options: It loses water by osmosis and shrinks until it breaks up
It actively pumps in water, using energy from respiration
It has a cellulose wall which is too weak to hold the cell
It gains water by osmosis and has no cell wall to stop it
scheme: Animal cells have no wall to resist swelling, so they can burst when water enters.

questions.prompt: Why is percentage change in mass calculated rather than change in mass?
options: It is quicker to calculate than the change in mass in grams
The pieces started with different masses
It removes the need to repeat the experiment several times
It always gives a bigger number that is easier to plot
scheme: Percentage change allows pieces with different starting masses to be compared fairly.

questions.prompt: What describes a plant cell that has lost a lot of water?
options: Turgid, because it has lost water and is full and firm
Burst, because the cell wall is torn open by the loss of water
Flaccid, because it has lost water and is no longer firm
Lysed, because the cell membrane is destroyed when water leaves
scheme: A plant cell that has lost a lot of water becomes flaccid; turgid cells are full of water.

questions.prompt: A potato cylinder has a mass of 3.20 g. After 30 minutes in a sugar solution its mass is 3.52 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
Explain why low oxygen availability can reduce mineral uptake by roots.
scheme: 1 · Less oxygen reduces aerobic respiration.
2 · Less energy is available for active transport.
3 · Mineral ions need to move against their concentration gradient.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between diffusion and active transport.
scheme: 1 · Diffusion is down a concentration gradient; active transport is against it.
2 · Diffusion is passive/needs no energy; active transport needs energy from respiration. Accept active transport uses carrier proteins.

questions.prompt: Waterlogged soil contains little oxygen. Explain why plants in waterlogged soil may show signs of mineral deficiency.
scheme: 1 · Root cells receive less oxygen.
2 · So less aerobic respiration / less energy released.
3 · Active transport of mineral ions needs energy.
4 · So fewer mineral ions (e.g. nitrate/magnesium) are absorbed against the gradient.

questions.prompt: Which process requires energy from respiration?
options: Osmosis, which uses energy from respiration to move water
Diffusion, which uses energy from respiration to move solutes
Evaporation, which uses energy from respiration to lose water
Active transport, which uses energy from respiration
scheme: Active transport needs energy from respiration; osmosis and diffusion are passive.

questions.prompt: Mineral concentration is lower in soil than a root cell. Uptake uses…
options: Active transport, using energy to move ions against the gradient
Diffusion, as ions move down the concentration gradient
Osmosis of ions, as water moves into the more dilute region
Evaporation of the ions from the surface of the root
scheme: Minerals are moved from a low concentration in the soil to a higher one in the root, which needs energy.

questions.prompt: What do carrier proteins do in active transport?
options: Digest particles so that they can pass through the membrane
Move particles across the membrane using energy from respiration
Make the membrane thicker so that the particles cannot escape
Store water so that the cell does not lose any by osmosis
scheme: Carrier proteins move substances across a membrane against the concentration gradient.

questions.prompt: Why do plants need nitrate ions?
options: To make chlorophyll only
To make glucose
To make cellulose
To make proteins
scheme: Nitrate supplies nitrogen for amino acids and proteins.

questions.prompt: Glucose is absorbed from the gut when its concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood. This uses…
options: osmosis, because it moves water across a membrane
diffusion, because it moves particles down a gradient
active transport, because it moves against the gradient
filtration, because it removes solid particles from a liquid
scheme: Movement against the concentration gradient requires active transport.

questions.prompt: Which process involves water moving through a partially permeable membrane?
options: Osmosis
Active transport
Respiration
Translocation
scheme: Osmosis is specific to water.

questions.prompt: The table shows ion concentrations in pond water and in the cells of a pond plant: nitrate 0.2 and 8.0 mmol/dm³. Calculate how many times greater the nitrate concentration is in the cells.
The table shows ion concentrations in pond water and in the cells of a pond plant: nitrate 0.2 and 8.0 mmol/dm³. Explain why the plant must use active transport to absorb nitrate.
scheme: 1 · the concentration is higher inside the cells, so it moves against the gradient

questions.prompt: The table shows ion concentrations in pond water and in the cells of a pond plant: nitrate 0.2 and 8.0 mmol/dm³. Suggest why the rate of nitrate uptake falls if the pond water is low in oxygen.
scheme: 1 · less aerobic respiration, so less energy for active transport

questions.prompt: Explain three precautions in preparing a bacterial culture.
scheme: 1 · Sterilise medium and equipment to remove contaminants.
2 · Minimise lid opening to reduce airborne contamination.
3 · Secure without fully sealing the lid and incubate at 25°C to reduce risk.

questions.prompt: A culture starts with 500 bacteria. The mean division time is 25 minutes. Calculate the number of bacteria after 150 minutes. Give your answer in standard form.
scheme: 1 · Number of divisions = 150 ÷ 25 = 6.

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the effect of three different antiseptics on the growth of bacteria.
scheme: 1 · Use sterile agar plate and spread bacteria evenly with sterile technique.
2 · Soak paper discs of the same size in each antiseptic.
3 · Include a control disc soaked in sterile water.
4 · Place discs on the agar, tape lid and incubate at 25 °C.
5 · Measure the diameter of each clear zone after a set time.
6 · Calculate area with πr² and compare; repeat for reliable means.

questions.prompt: A clear circle has diameter 10 mm. Use π = 3.14 to calculate area.
scheme: Radius 5 mm; 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 mm².

questions.prompt: Why incubate school cultures at 25°C?
options: To sterilise the agar so that nothing can grow on it
Because no bacteria can grow at all at 37 °C
To make the bacteria grow as quickly as possible
To reduce the risk of growing harmful pathogens
scheme: At 25 °C the bacteria that grow are less likely to be harmful to humans than those that grow at body temperature.

questions.prompt: Why is the inoculating loop passed through a flame?
options: To make it bend into the right shape to spread bacteria
To kill microorganisms that are on it before it is used
To dry it so that the agar is not damaged by moisture
To warm the agar so that the bacteria grow faster
scheme: Flaming sterilises the loop so it does not add unwanted microorganisms.

questions.prompt: Why is the Petri dish lid taped but not sealed all round?
options: So that the lid falls off if the bacteria grow too quickly
So that bacteria can escape and spread through the laboratory
So that oxygen can enter and harmful anaerobic bacteria are not encouraged
So that water can drain out of the dish onto the bench
scheme: Taping the lid in a few places lets air in, which prevents harmful anaerobic bacteria from growing.

questions.prompt: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are produced from one after 2 hours?
scheme: 2 hours = 6 divisions; 2⁶ = 64.

questions.prompt: How do bacteria reproduce?
options: Meiosis
Mitosis with gametes
Binary fission
Budding of spores only
scheme: Bacteria divide by binary fission.

b-review-cells.title: Cell biology: review and exam practice

questions.prompt: A student views onion cells. Describe how to prepare the slide and focus on the cells.
scheme: 1 · Peel thin layer of onion epidermis and place on slide in a drop of water/iodine.
2 · Lower coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.
3 · Start with the lowest-power objective.
4 · Use coarse focus then fine focus to get a clear image.

questions.prompt: A cell measures 0.05 mm. A student's drawing of the cell is 25 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
Compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
scheme: 1 · Diffusion: net movement of particles from high to low concentration.
2 · Diffusion is passive / needs no energy.
3 · Osmosis: movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.
4 · From dilute to concentrated solution, passive.
5 · Active transport moves substances against a gradient.
6 · Needs energy from respiration / uses carrier proteins, e.g. mineral uptake by roots.

questions.prompt: Explain why a multicellular organism needs exchange surfaces and a transport system.
scheme: 1 · Large organisms have a small SA:V.
2 · Diffusion alone is too slow over long distances to supply all cells.
3 · Exchange surfaces increase area; transport system carries substances to cells.

questions.prompt: Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?
options: The cell membrane, which is partially permeable
The cell wall, which is made of cellulose in plants
The nucleus, which contains the genetic material
The ribosome, which is where proteins are made
scheme: The membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.

questions.prompt: An image is 4.8 mm long at × 400. What is the real length?
options: 12 μm
120 μm

questions.prompt: Which cell type is specialised to carry impulses?
options: Sperm cell
Root hair cell
Xylem
Nerve cell
scheme: Nerve cells have long axons.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of mitosis in adults?
options: Making gametes that are genetically different from each other
Producing variation so that the cells are all different
Repair and replacement of damaged or worn-out cells
Digestion of food molecules inside the cells of the gut
scheme: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells for growth, repair and replacement.

questions.prompt: Stem cells from embryos can…
options: only make blood cells and no other kind of cell
differentiate into most types of body cell
not divide, because they are already specialised
only form plant tissue and not animal tissue
scheme: Embryonic stem cells are unspecialised and can become most cell types.

questions.prompt: Which process moves glucose from a low concentration in the gut into the blood?
options: Diffusion, which moves particles down a concentration gradient
Osmosis, which is the movement of water across a membrane
Transpiration, which is the loss of water from the leaves
Active transport, which uses energy to move against a gradient
scheme: Moving glucose from a low to a high concentration is against the gradient, so it needs active transport.

questions.prompt: A cube of side 4 cm has SA:V of…
A potato piece changes from 5.0 g to 5.6 g. Percentage change?
Why do electron microscopes show more detail?
options: Higher resolution
They use coloured light
They are bigger
They use living cells
scheme: Resolution determines detail.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT found in a bacterial cell?
options: Ribosomes
Cell membrane
Mitochondria
Cytoplasm
scheme: Prokaryotes lack mitochondria.

questions.prompt: Explain how bile assists fat digestion.
scheme: 1 · It neutralises acid, providing alkaline conditions for lipase.
2 · It emulsifies fat into smaller droplets.
3 · This increases surface area available to lipase.

questions.prompt: Give the level of organisation of the stomach and explain your answer.
scheme: 1 · Organ.
2 · It is made of several tissues (e.g. muscle, glandular, epithelial) working together for a function.

questions.prompt: Describe how a protein in food is digested and how the products are used in the body.
scheme: 1 · Protease/pepsin in the stomach begins breaking protein down.
2 · Proteases from the pancreas/small intestine complete digestion to amino acids.
3 · Amino acids are absorbed into the blood through the villi/small intestine wall.
4 · Amino acids are used to build new proteins (e.g. enzymes, muscle).

questions.prompt: Protein digestion produces…
options: Starch, which is stored in the liver as a food reserve
Amino acids, which are absorbed into the blood
Only fatty acids, which are absorbed into the lymph
Glucose, which is then used in respiration by the cells
scheme: Proteases break proteins down into amino acids.

questions.prompt: Where is bile made?
options: The liver, which stores the bile in the gall bladder
The gall bladder, which releases the bile into the gut
The stomach, which mixes the bile with the food
The pancreas, which releases the bile into the small intestine
scheme: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder until it is released.

questions.prompt: Which organ produces lipase, protease and amylase?
options: Liver
Gall bladder
Large intestine
Pancreas
scheme: The pancreas secretes all three.

questions.prompt: Why does the stomach contain hydrochloric acid?
options: To digest fat so that it can be absorbed in the small intestine
To emulsify fat so that lipase has a larger surface area
To kill microorganisms and give the low pH that pepsin needs
To absorb water from the food before it reaches the intestine
scheme: Acid kills pathogens that are swallowed with food and gives the stomach protease the low pH it works best at.

questions.prompt: What are the products of lipid digestion?
options: Amino acids, which are released when proteases act on the lipids
Fatty acids and glycerol
Simple sugars, which are made when carbohydrases act on the lipids
Glycogen, which is stored in the liver after the lipids are digested
scheme: Lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.prompt: Where is most water absorbed?
options: The stomach, which absorbs most of the water that is swallowed
The oesophagus, which absorbs water as the food passes through
The mouth, which absorbs water from the saliva that is produced
The large intestine
scheme: The large intestine absorbs water from the undigested material that is left, leaving the faeces.

questions.prompt: A student mixes milk with lipase and measures the pH as the fat is digested. Explain why the pH decreases.
scheme: 1 · lipase breaks down fat into fatty acids and glycerol
1 · fatty acids are acidic / lower the pH

questions.prompt: A student mixes milk with lipase and measures the pH as the fat is digested. Predict and explain the effect of adding bile to the mixture.

questions.prompt: What makes targeted binding possible?

The specificity of an antibody for one particular antigen
An equal binding of the antibody to every other molecule
The large size of the antibody compared with the antigen

Two sperm cells from the same male
A mouse lymphocyte and a tumour cell
A stem cell and a platelet from the blood

Oestrogen
Adrenaline
hCG

It is not toxic to any of the cells in the body
It binds only to cells with a specific antigen
It stays in the stomach where it cannot reach healthy cells

questions.prompt: A disadvantage of monoclonal antibodies is that they…

can cause more side effects than were expected
work on every disease that a doctor might treat
are cheap compared with other treatments for cancer

questions.prompt: Explain why yellow leaves do not prove infection and suggest an alternative explanation and investigation.

questions.prompt: Give two ways a gardener could identify the disease affecting a plant.
scheme: 1 · Use a gardening manual/website.

questions.prompt: Describe the physical, chemical and mechanical defences of plants and explain how each protects the plant.

Carbon dioxide, which is needed in the air around the leaf

A waxy cuticle that covers the surface of the leaf

Purple flowers
More chlorophyll
Thicker bark

questions.prompt: Which is a mechanical defence?

Thorns
Antibacterial chemicals
Cellulose wall

They feed on sap from the phloem and can spread pathogens
They eat the chlorophyll in the cells of the leaf

A high level of humidity, which encourages fungal growth
A shortage of magnesium

questions.prompt: Describe how malaria is spread and two ways of reducing its spread.

questions.prompt: Explain how white blood cells defend the body against pathogens.

2 · Produce antibodies.
3 · Antibodies specific to antigens on pathogen.

scheme: 1 · Drug tested on cells/tissues in the lab (preclinical).

5 · Double-blind trials with a placebo group.

questions.prompt: Which disease is caused by a protist?

HIV
Malaria
Gonorrhoea

questions.prompt: Tobacco mosaic virus affects…

plants
fish
bacteria

Make antigens

To reduce the cost of carrying out a clinical trial

Malaria

viruses, which replace the ones that are already there
antibodies and memory cells

Viruses have no DNA or RNA that a drug could target
Viruses are bacteria, which no drug can kill

Low doses of the drug being used by mistake
Review by other scientists before publication

They are vaccines that give long-term immunity

The time of day at which the test is carried out

To change the independent variable for each person

The damage never affects the behaviour of the patient

MRI scanning

Only the structure of the brain, not how it works

The risk of irreversible harm and the need for consent

questions.prompt: Describe how an eye focuses on a nearby object.

2 · Suspensory ligaments become tight / pulled taut.

Contract, so that the suspensory ligaments become slack
Become the pupil, so that more light is let in
Move the lens backwards so that it is closer to the retina

A convex lens, which brings the light rays together
A flat window, which does not change the light rays at all
A prism, which splits the light into different colours

Carries the impulses to the brain along the optic nerve
Changes the size of the pupil in bright light
Refracts light into the eye

questions.prompt: In dim light the pupil…

closes
gets larger
stays the same

tight, making the lens thin
cut
relaxed and the lens fat

questions.prompt: Long sight (hyperopia) is corrected with a…

concave lens
flat lens
mirror

questions.prompt: Describe three responses to low core temperature.
scheme: 1 · Skin blood vessels constrict.
2 · Sweating decreases or stops.
3 · Skeletal muscles contract repeatedly, causing shivering.

questions.prompt: Explain why it is important to keep core body temperature at about 37 °C.
scheme: 1 · This is the optimum temperature for enzymes.
2 · Too high denatures enzymes / too low slows reactions.

questions.prompt: Describe how the body detects and responds to an increase in core temperature.
scheme: 1 · Thermoregulatory centre/hypothalamus detects blood temperature rise.
2 · Skin receptors send impulses to the thermoregulatory centre.
3 · Sweat glands secrete more sweat.
4 · Blood vessels supplying skin capillaries dilate.

questions.prompt: Which occurs when too warm?
options: Increased sweating, which transfers energy from the skin
Increased shivering, which releases energy in the muscles
Constriction of all of the skin blood vessels
Body hairs standing on end to trap a layer of air
scheme: When the body is too warm, sweating and vasodilation help to lose energy.

questions.prompt: Where is the thermoregulatory centre?
options: The pancreas, where the hormones are made in the body
The bladder, where the urine is stored before it is removed
The skin, where the temperature receptors are found
The brain, where the hypothalamus monitors the blood temperature
scheme: The thermoregulatory centre is in the brain; it receives information from receptors in the skin and blood.

questions.prompt: What is the normal human core temperature?
options: About 30 °C
About 37 °C
About 40 °C
About 25 °C
scheme: Body temperature is kept near 37 °C.

questions.prompt: Which response happens when the body is too cold?
options: Shivering
Sweating more
Vasodilation
Panting
scheme: Shivering increases respiration.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain contains the thermoregulatory centre?
options: Cerebellum
Medulla
Hypothalamus
Cortex
scheme: The hypothalamus monitors blood temperature.

questions.prompt: Why can very high body temperatures be dangerous?
options: Blood freezes
Sweat stops
Cells stop needing oxygen
Enzymes denature
scheme: Enzymes are sensitive to temperature.

questions.prompt: A person moves from a warm room into a very cold place. Name the part of the brain that detects the change in blood temperature.

questions.prompt: Explain how shivering and vasoconstriction help in cold conditions.

2 · More energy is transferred to thermal stores.
3 · Vasoconstriction reduces skin blood flow and transfer to surroundings.

questions.prompt: Explain why a person's skin looks pale on a very cold day.
scheme: 1 · Blood vessels supplying skin capillaries constrict.
2 · Less blood flows near the skin surface.

scheme: 1 · Thermoregulatory centre detects drop in blood temperature.

questions.prompt: Why does sweat evaporation cool skin?

The heat is made when the sweat glands start to respire
Energy is transferred from the skin to the evaporating sweat
The sweat pushes warm blood further away from the surface
scheme: Evaporation takes energy from the skin, so it is cooled.

questions.prompt: Vasoconstriction conserves energy because…

Less warm blood flows near the surface of the skin
The heart stops beating for a short time to save energy
More sweat is made by the sweat glands to cool the skin
scheme: Vasoconstriction narrows skin blood vessels, so less energy is transferred to the surroundings.

questions.prompt: Why is sweating less effective in humid air?
options: Less sweat evaporates
More sweat is made
Blood vessels constrict
Skin is colder
scheme: High humidity reduces evaporation.

questions.prompt: How does vasodilation cool the body?
options: The vessels move closer to the skin so that they lose heat
More blood flows near the skin surface
It reduces the amount of sweating that takes place
It increases the shivering of the muscles in the skin
scheme: Vasodilation increases the blood flow to the skin capillaries, so more energy is transferred to the surroundings.

questions.prompt: Why does shivering warm the body?
options: It reduces the blood flow to the surface of the skin

Muscle contraction increases respiration, releasing energy as heat
It lowers the metabolic rate so that less heat is lost
scheme: Respiration in the muscles is exothermic, so shivering transfers energy to the body.

To kill any bacteria that are in the patient's blood
To keep the blood warm as it flows through the machine

Less urine that is more concentrated

questions.prompt: Which method is permanent?

Giving bacteria a human insulin gene so they make insulin

The plants grow taller and so receive more light than weeds

Modifying an organism's genome by adding a gene from another organism
Cloning a plant by taking a cutting from the parent
Crossing two different species to produce a hybrid

questions.prompt: Golden rice was modified to contain…

insulin
pesticide
more water

options: Using drugs to kill the bacteria that cause a disease
Selective breeding of a crop for a desired feature
Adding working alleles to treat an inherited disorder

questions.prompt: Which is a concern about GM crops?

They cannot be eaten
They always reduce yields
Genes may spread to wild plants

Provides all of the energy that the new cell needs to grow
Destroys every other gene in the cell once it has entered
Cuts the DNA at a specific base sequence at its recognition site

Only a ruler, which is used to cut the DNA at the gene
Antibodies, which are used to bind to the gene in the DNA

Proteases, which break down proteins into amino acids
Restriction enzymes

questions.prompt: Which enzymes join DNA fragments?

Ligases
Lipases
Carbohydrases

questions.prompt: Why are genes put into animal cells at an early stage of development?

To make the cells divide faster so the animal grows more
To avoid having to use a vector to carry the gene
So that the cells become bacteria that make the protein

questions.prompt: A plasmid is used as a…
options: host
enzyme
vector
marker only
scheme: Plasmids carry genes into cells.

questions.prompt: Explain one benefit and two risks of growing cloned crops.

questions.prompt: Give two advantages of taking cuttings compared with growing plants from seed.
scheme: 1 · Quicker/cheaper.
2 · Offspring identical so desirable features are kept.

questions.prompt: Describe the process of adult cell cloning and give one benefit and one concern.
scheme: 1 · Nucleus removed from an unfertilised egg cell.

questions.prompt: Which uses small plant cell groups in sterile medium?
options: Meiosis, which uses the sex cells of the parent plants
Pollination, which uses pollen from other plants
Grafting, which joins a shoot onto the root of another plant
Tissue culture, which uses small groups of plant cells
scheme: Tissue culture grows plants from small groups of cells in a sterile medium with nutrients and hormones.

questions.prompt: A clone’s nuclear DNA matches…
options: The donor of the body-cell nucleus that was used
All of the donors equally, since the cells are mixed together
The host animal that carries the clone during the pregnancy
The animal that provided the egg cell with its nucleus removed

questions.prompt: What is removed from the egg cell in adult cell cloning?

The nucleus
The membrane
Mitochondria

questions.prompt: How is the cloned cell stimulated to divide?

Fertilisation by sperm
Adding hormones only
Heating

questions.prompt: Which method produces many plants from a few cells on a nutrient medium?
options: Embryo transplant
Selective breeding
Tissue culture
Adult cell cloning

questions.prompt: Embryo transplants use cells from embryos…
options: before they specialise
after the animal has been born and has grown up
from adults that have already finished their development
from bacteria that have been grown in the laboratory

questions.prompt: A farmer uses embryo transplants to produce several calves from a prize cow and bull. Explain why the calves are genetically identical to each other but not to either parent.

questions.prompt: Explain speciation following geographical isolation.

scheme: 1 · Chromosomes, genes and DNA had not been discovered.

questions.prompt: Compare the theories of Darwin and Lamarck, and explain why Darwin's theory is now accepted.

options: The mechanisms of inheritance were not yet known
No variation existed between members of the same species
All of the fossils that had been found were still living
The theory had not been published in a scientific journal

questions.prompt: Species are separated in the usual reproductive model when…

questions.prompt: Which scientist published 'On the Origin of Species'?
options: Gregor Mendel
Charles Darwin
Alfred Russel Wallace
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck

DNA is a double helix made of two strands
Changes acquired during life are passed on to the offspring
Genes are found on the chromosomes in the nucleus

finches
bacteria
pea plants

Rocks only preserve the remains of living cells and tissue

A long root that reaches water deep underground
